prompt.context: Stefan Lessard, the CEO of a large conglomerate, finds a once-in-a-lifetime deal and buys a satellite at a heavily discounted price. He can keep it or sell it today for a profit.
prompt.question: What questions could you ask to gain critical information? Then determine the best road to profits for DMB Satellite.

clarifying_info.q: How much did DMB pay for the satellite?
What is the satellite worth today if sold?
clarifying_info.a: The market value today is $35 million.

clarifying_info.q: What are the repair or maintenance costs?
clarifying_info.a: Negligible. The satellite is in good condition.
No. It is still in the box and needs to be launched if the company decides to keep it. After launch it can be used for 3 years, after which it becomes obsolete with $0 resale value.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to launch the satellite?
clarifying_info.a: $10 million for a high orbit launch and $8 million for a low orbit launch.

clarifying_info.q: What is the difference between low orbit and high orbit?
clarifying_info.a: Low orbit satellites transmit data between two points 3,000-5,000 miles apart (coast to coast). They are primarily used by corporations to transmit data in batches. Low orbit signal has high interference and is not used when continuous transmission quality is critical. High orbit satellites are used for continuous real-time transmission where signal quality is critical; live global television broadcasting is the primary application.

Two segments: (1) Large corporations that batch-transfer data periodically — short and intermittent use, allowing multiple clients on the same satellite. (2) News broadcasters and telecommunications companies needing voice/video transmission with 24-hour global coverage — this limits the satellite to only one client.
Leasing capacity is a good option in general but is not available in this case.

clarifying_info.q: What is the life expectancy of the satellite?
clarifying_info.a: 5 years total, though it can only be used for 3 years after launch before becoming obsolete.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue rates for the low orbit (data transmission) option?
clarifying_info.a: Each Year 1 customer pays $50,000 per month. Each Year 2 customer pays $30,000 per month. Each Year 3 customer pays $20,000 per month. Prices fall to new rates for existing contracts in the following year. 80% of customers from a given year will remain the following year.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers can be expected each year for the low orbit option?
clarifying_info.a: Year 1: 50 new customers; Year 2: 40 new customers; Year 3: 30 new customers.

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue rates for the high orbit (voice/video) option?
clarifying_info.a: The single high orbit customer pays $2,500,000 per month under a 3-year contract.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have access to capital for the satellite purchase and launch?
clarifying_info.a: (Interviewer: confirm that the candidate raises this question; assume yes for analysis purposes.)

framework: Identify the three mutually exclusive options: (1) Sell satellite today, (2) Keep and launch in low orbit for multi-client data transmission, (3) Keep and launch in high orbit for single-client voice/video transmission
For each option, calculate total revenue over the satellite's useful life and subtract all relevant costs to arrive at pre-tax profit
Compare profits across all three options on a like-for-like basis
Assess qualitative risks and strategic fit for each option (capital requirements, customer concentration, market dynamics)
Deliver a bottom-line recommendation with supporting rationale

questions.prompt: Option 1 — Sell today: What is the profit if DMB sells the satellite immediately?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize the $10M acquisition cost is a sunk cost and should NOT be subtracted from the sale proceeds. Profit = sale price minus acquisition cost only if framed as investment return; the incremental decision profit is simply the $35M market value received. The casebook frames it as $35M pre-tax profit (implicitly treating the $10M as already spent).

math.setup: Sale price = $35M; acquisition cost = $10M (sunk cost). Pre-tax profit = $35M - $10M = $25M net gain, but the casebook states $35M profit recognizing the sunk cost framing.
steps: Pre-tax profit = $35,000,000 (casebook frames the full sale price as the profit figure, noting sunk cost)

questions.prompt: Option 2 — Low orbit multi-client data transmission: What is the 3-year profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate must track three cohorts of new customers across three years, apply the 80% retention rate to compute revenue, then subtract the $8M low orbit launch cost. Key insight: prices fall each year and existing contracts reprice to the new year rate. New customers in Y1=50, Y2=40, Y3=30. The analysis table in the casebook shows ~$85.2M total revenue and ~$77.2M rounded profit; the summary page states $73,360,000 profit. Use the summary figure as authoritative.

math.setup: New customers: Y1=50 @$50K/mo, Y2=40 @$30K/mo, Y3=30 @$20K/mo. Retention: 80% of prior year customers carry forward at the new year price. All months = 12. Launch cost = $8M.
steps: Y1 revenue: 50 customers x $50,000/mo x 12 mo = $30,000,000
Y2 retained from Y1: 50 x 80% = 40 customers; Y2 new: 40 customers; Total Y2 customers = 80 @ $30,000/mo x 12 = $28,800,000

Y3 retained from Y2 cohort (40 x 80% = 32) + retained from Y1 cohort still active (40 x 80% = 32): Total Y3 customers ~62 @ $20,000/mo x 12. Casebook simplifies: Y3 revenue shown as $7,200,000 for the 30-new-customer row.

questions.prompt: Option 3 — High orbit single-client voice/video transmission: What is the 3-year profit?
questions.guidance: One customer, fixed monthly rate of $2.5M, 3-year contract, 36 months. Subtract $10M high orbit launch cost. Straightforward calculation. Note the risk: single customer means high concentration risk.

math.setup: 1 customer x $2,500,000/mo x 36 months = $90,000,000 total revenue. Launch cost = $10,000,000.

questions.prompt: Capital check: What important qualifier must the candidate raise before recommending Options 2 or 3?
questions.guidance: The candidate must verify that DMB has access to the capital required for both the satellite purchase ($10M already paid) and the launch cost ($8M or $10M). Failing to raise this is noted as a gap in the performance evaluation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks and considerations for each of the three options?

categories.name: Option 1 — Sell today
ideas: No operational complexity or launch risk
Sunk cost of $10M acquisition should not affect the sell decision
Must assess whether there are better reinvestment opportunities for the $35M
Market value may rise or fall — timing matters

categories.name: Option 2 — Low orbit multi-client
ideas: Diversified customer portfolio reduces concentration risk
Revenue declines each year as competition enters and prices fall

categories.name: Option 3 — High orbit single-client
ideas: Highest absolute profit ($80M) among the three
Extreme customer concentration — losing the one client is catastrophic
Client has strong bargaining power given exclusivity
Risk of client bankruptcy or contract default
Specialized market with very few available customers
Higher launch investment ($10M) with binary outcome

recommendation: Option 2 (low orbit, multi-client data transmission) is the recommended path, generating ~$73M pre-tax profit over 3 years
It provides a diversified revenue base across multiple corporate clients, reducing the catastrophic downside risk of a single-client dependency
While Option 3 generates the highest profit ($80M), the risk profile is unacceptably concentrated in one customer
Option 1 (sell today for $35M) is the weakest financially unless DMB lacks the capital for launch or has no appetite for operational risk
risks: Option 3: Single client could go bankrupt, renegotiate, or cancel, eliminating all revenue
Option 3: Client holds strong bargaining power in contract renewals
Option 2: Competitive pricing pressure erodes revenues year over year
Option 2: 20% annual customer churn requires continuous sales effort
Both launch options: DMB must confirm access to capital before committing
All options: $10M acquisition cost is sunk and should not drive the decision
next_steps: Confirm DMB has capital for satellite purchase and launch before committing
If pursuing Option 2, begin customer acquisition immediately to maximize Year 1 cohort
Conduct due diligence on the single high-orbit customer's creditworthiness before reconsidering Option 3
Monitor competitive satellite launches that could accelerate price erosion in the data-transmission market
